labGuides.title: See how a controller changes mechanism response
labGuides.outcome: Relate proportional, integral, derivative, and feedforward terms to a simplified response plot.
beforeYouStart: This teaching model is not the production controller.
Keep the displayed response bounded.
tryThis: Run the baseline and note rise time, overshoot, and final error.
Change only one gain, predict what will happen, then run again.
Restore the baseline before comparing a different gain.
reflectionQuestions: Which measurement changed in the direction you predicted?
What evidence would you still need before proposing a robot tuning change?
labGuides.successLooksLike: You can describe one tradeoff using the plotted evidence without claiming the values are safe for hardware.

labGuides.title: Meet a response goal without hiding the model
labGuides.outcome: Use proportional, derivative, velocity-feedforward, and gravity-feedforward terms to meet bounded goals in three simplified mechanism models.
beforeYouStart: These normalized plants are not a digital twin of your robot.
The lab never writes gains to a project or commands hardware.
tryThis: Choose one mechanism and record the baseline rise, overshoot, settling, and final-error evidence.
Change one term, predict one metric, and compare the result.
Open the Subsystem Builder control step and identify where reviewed gains would live in the generated contract.
reflectionQuestions: Which term changed the response in the direction you predicted?
What measured units, mechanism constants, current limits, and test plan are still required before tuning a robot?
labGuides.successLooksLike: You can meet a teaching-model goal and explain why the result is not a hardware-safe gain recommendation.

labGuides.title: Combine imperfect position estimates
labGuides.outcome: See why odometry drift, measurement noise, and uncertainty affect a fused estimate.
beforeYouStart: This is a simplified diagonal teaching filter, not the production ARES EKF.
tryThis: Compare truth, drifting odometry, and the fused estimate.
Increase one uncertainty and predict which source the estimate will trust less.
Reset and compare the same time window again.
reflectionQuestions: Why can a smooth estimate still be wrong?
Which timestamp, frame, and units would a real vision measurement need?
labGuides.successLooksLike: You can explain that fusion weighs uncertain evidence; it does not turn a sensor into ground truth.

labGuides.title: Turn a chassis request into wheel or module targets
labGuides.outcome: Use the production ARES inverse-kinematics math to compare mecanum wheel speeds and swerve module speed/azimuth targets.
beforeYouStart: Robot-frame +X is forward, +Y is left, and positive rotation is counter-clockwise.
Ideal kinematics omit traction, motor dynamics, steering delay, voltage, current, and field obstacles.
tryThis: Request pure forward, pure left strafe, and pure counter-clockwise rotation.
Combine translation and rotation until uniform wheel-speed scaling appears.
Open the Drivebase Builder and connect track width, wheelbase, inversion, and maximum speed to the preview inputs.
reflectionQuestions: Why must every wheel target be scaled by the same factor?
Which physical effects could make measured robot motion differ from the ideal target?
labGuides.successLooksLike: You can predict one wheel/module pattern and name at least two omitted physical effects.

labGuides.title: Trade speed for acceleration and smoothness
labGuides.outcome: Compare bounded motion profiles before using them in an autonomous routine.
beforeYouStart: The profile is a teaching preview and does not prove field clearance or traction.
tryThis: Start with the conservative preset and inspect position, velocity, and acceleration.
Change one limit and predict how total time changes.
Compare the result with the robot's documented speed and acceleration envelope.
reflectionQuestions: Which constraint limited the move?
What robot or field evidence is missing from this one-dimensional model?
labGuides.successLooksLike: You can explain how one constraint changed the profile without calling the preview a validated autonomous path.

labGuides.title: Estimate mechanism load and speed
labGuides.outcome: Explore how geometry, gearing, mass, and efficiency affect a simplified mechanism estimate.
beforeYouStart: Use measured units where possible.
A simplified estimate cannot replace vendor limits or a mechanical review.
tryThis: Choose a mechanism and record the baseline load and speed estimate.
Change gearing or geometry while holding every other input constant.
Check whether the result stays inside the stated model assumptions.
reflectionQuestions: Which input had the largest effect?
What current, thermal, structural, or friction evidence would a real design still need?
labGuides.successLooksLike: You can use the estimate to ask a better design question, not to certify a mechanism.

labGuides.title: Decide when a mechanism is safe to move
labGuides.outcome: Use cached, fresh evidence to establish home and recover a latched output fault through a confirmed neutral write.
beforeYouStart: This is a hardware-free teaching model, not a production subsystem controller.
A home sensor, current spike, or stopped motor is evidence only when its cached measurement is valid and fresh.
tryThis: Establish home with a digital sensor and the required evidence dwell.
Switch to current, velocity, and combined stall evidence; make one required measurement invalid or stale.
Latch a failed output write, attempt a failed neutral recovery, then allow the neutral write to succeed.
reflectionQuestions: Why should one high-current sample not establish home?
Which conditions must still be checked after a home reference exists?
Why does clearing a fault require evidence that neutral output was actually written?
labGuides.successLooksLike: You can explain freshness, dwell, homing evidence, fault latching, and neutral recovery without treating the model as hardware approval.

labGuides.title: Trace one signal through ARES
labGuides.outcome: Follow controller or sensor input through typed actions, immutable Redux state, a controller, mock IO, and unit-tagged telemetry.
beforeYouStart: This is a simplified teaching trace, not the production Redux store or robot runtime.
Read the unit and validity text at every stage instead of relying on color.
tryThis: Run a motor command and compare the retained previous state with the reducer's new state.
Invert a positional servo, then predict the normalized position before running the loop.
Make a motor measurement stale and a distance sample invalid; explain why the resulting behavior differs.
reflectionQuestions: Why must the reducer create a new state instead of mutating the previous snapshot?
Which stage decides what the robot wants, and which stage touches hardware?
Why do a topic name, value, unit, timestamp, and validity belong together?
labGuides.successLooksLike: You can narrate input -> action -> reducer -> immutable state -> controller -> IO -> telemetry and identify the unit and safety boundary at each step.

labGuides.title: Validate a small autonomous plan before generation
labGuides.outcome: Reason about starting pose, field bounds, resources, conditions, timeouts, and failure behavior without saving or running a routine.
beforeYouStart: This is a two-step teaching model, not the production routine validator or simulator.
Preview readiness does not prove collision clearance, traction, wiring, or physical safety.
tryThis: Move the starting or target pose until part of the robot footprint leaves the field, then read the blocking reason.
Shorten the timeout below the ideal drive estimate plus margin.
Create a parallel resource conflict, then repair it without deleting either intended behavior.
Compare stop-and-report with continue-on-failure for a required versus explicitly optional action.
reflectionQuestions: Why is a robot-center coordinate inside the field insufficient by itself?
What does a timeout protect, and what can it not prove?
Why must parallel routine branches declare exclusive resources and explicit failure behavior?
labGuides.successLooksLike: You can explain why a plan is preview-ready or blocked, then carry the same checks into the real routine builder.

lessons.title: Launch Simulator & Drivetrain Telemetry
lessons.outcome: Start the platform-appropriate local physics simulator, drive a supported chassis with live gamepad/keyboard input, and observe CCW+ heading and wheel speed telemetry.
beforeYouStart: Open a configured FTC, FRC, or XRP project workspace.
No robot hardware is required.
steps: Select Local Sim in the execution toolbar.
Choose Start simulator and wait for the status to become connected.
Open Dashboard and find pose, motor, and system-health telemetry.
Drive with WASD or a connected USB gamepad to observe the configured chassis motion.
Stop the simulator when you finish so no background process remains.
lessons.successLooksLike: The app reports a local simulator connection, chassis speeds reflect driver input, and dashboard telemetry updates in real time.
lessons.safetyNote: Simulator commands never authorize a physical robot. Confirm the target says Local Sim.

checkpoints.title: Select Local Sim
checkpoints.instruction: Choose Local Sim in the execution toolbar before launching anything.
checkpoints.successText: Local Sim is the selected execution target.

checkpoints.title: Start the simulator
checkpoints.instruction: Launch one simulator and keep its terminal output visible.
checkpoints.successText: ARES can see its managed simulator process running.

checkpoints.title: Wait for local telemetry
checkpoints.instruction: Wait until the local simulator and NT4 connection both report ready.
checkpoints.successText: ARES observes an NT4 connection to the local simulator.

checkpoints.title: Name the data source
checkpoints.instruction: Open Dashboard, find one changing value, and say that it is live simulator data—not replay and not a physical robot.
checkpoints.successText: You identified the source, one changing value, and its meaning.

checkpoints.title: Stop the simulator
checkpoints.instruction: Use the Analytics Stop action and confirm the managed simulator process ends.
checkpoints.successText: ARES no longer sees the simulator process. This does not indicate a physical robot's enabled state.

lessons.title: Build a Drivebase Blueprint
lessons.outcome: Create the supported drivetrain for this workspace, name its hardware, describe geometry and localization, choose control modes, and review safety before saving.
beforeYouStart: Have the hardware names or CAN IDs, wheel diameter, track width, and wheelbase available if this is a real robot design.
steps: Open Drivebase Builder and choose a template marked NO-CODE RUNNABLE for the active FTC or FRC workspace.
Enter the exact FTC Robot Controller names or FRC CAN IDs and bus names, then review each inversion setting.
Enter measured geometry and select the sensors that provide heading and position.
Choose open-loop, wheel-velocity, chassis-velocity, or trajectory control only when its required feedback is available.
Use the offline drive-control lab to predict wheel or module commands. The lab never commands hardware.
Review braking, current monitoring, fault behavior, and the structured diff before saving the canonical document.
lessons.successLooksLike: The canonical drivebase document validates, every hardware address is explicit, and you can explain the selected control and safety contracts.
lessons.safetyNote: The offline lab verifies document math, not wiring. Physical direction checks require a restrained robot and an acknowledged robot-side test protocol.

checkpoints.title: Select drivetrain architecture
checkpoints.instruction: Choose Mecanum or Swerve based on your season's robot chassis.
checkpoints.successText: Drivebase architecture is declared.

checkpoints.title: Set geometric dimensions
checkpoints.instruction: Specify track width and wheelbase in millimeters or inches.
checkpoints.successText: Physical drivebase dimensions are declared and non-zero.

checkpoints.title: Save drivebase blueprint
checkpoints.instruction: Save the completed drivebase configuration document to the workspace.
checkpoints.successText: Canonical drivebase blueprint is saved and ready for code generation.

lessons.title: Inverse Kinematics & Desaturation Lab
lessons.outcome: Calculate wheel speed vectors from chassis speeds (vx, vy, omega) and explore uniform desaturation scaling under saturation.
beforeYouStart: ARES coordinate convention: +X forward, +Y left (blue wall), positive rotation counter-clockwise (CCW+).
steps: Open the Drive Kinematics interactive lab.
Apply pure forward translation (vx = 1.0 m/s) and verify all wheels rotate forward.
Apply pure lateral strafe (vy = 1.0 m/s) and observe diagonal wheel speed inversions.
Combine translation and high rotation until wheel speeds exceed physical motor limits.
Observe how desaturation preserves trajectory direction by scaling all wheel velocities uniformly.
lessons.successLooksLike: You can predict individual wheel velocity vectors for any chassis speed command and explain the importance of uniform desaturation.
lessons.safetyNote: Non-uniform wheel speed clipping changes the robot's heading uncontrollably during high-speed translation.

checkpoints.title: Explain uniform desaturation
checkpoints.instruction: Why must all wheel speed targets be scaled by the same factor when any single wheel saturates?
checkpoints.successText: You recorded the engineering explanation in your own words and verified the supporting tool evidence.

lessons.title: EKF Odometry & AprilTag Fusion Lab
lessons.outcome: Compare drifting deadwheel odometry with periodic AprilTag vision pose estimates and Mahalanobis rejection gating.
beforeYouStart: Deadwheels provide high-frequency relative tracking but accumulate slip drift over time.
AprilTags provide absolute field references but have latency and measurement noise.
steps: Open the Sensor Fusion interactive lab.
Run the simulation with pure odometry and observe drift accumulation over multiple laps.
Enable AprilTag vision measurement updates and observe how the EKF pulls estimated pose back to ground truth.
Inject high-noise vision outliers and observe Mahalanobis distance gating reject false measurements.
Tune vision covariance matrices to balance tracking smoothness with correction responsiveness.
lessons.successLooksLike: You can explain how the Extended Kalman Filter weighs odometry uncertainty against vision measurement variance.
lessons.safetyNote: Never rely on raw vision snaps during active motion without Mahalanobis gating; camera glares can cause sudden violent pose jumps.

checkpoints.title: Explain sensor weighting
checkpoints.instruction: How does the EKF use measurement covariance matrices to decide whether to trust odometry or vision?
checkpoints.successText: You recorded the engineering explanation in your own words and verified the supporting tool evidence.

lessons.title: Build a Safe Mechanism Subsystem
lessons.outcome: Start from a mechanism template, connect cached hardware signals to immutable state, select a supported controller and feedforward model, and define fail-closed behavior.
beforeYouStart: Know what the mechanism should do and which motors, servos, and sensors are actually present. Exact gains are not required yet.
steps: Open Subsystem Builder and choose the closest capability template. Prefer a concrete mechanism or typed sensor starter over Advanced/custom.

Give every motor, servo, encoder, distance sensor, IMU, or pneumatic device its exact address, direction, safe neutral, leader/follower relationship, and cached input signals. For an FTC IMU, describe the Control Hub logo and USB orientation.

Explain which immutable values are requested targets and which are cached measurements, then connect them to direct, position PID, profiled position PID, velocity PID, bang-bang, or servo-position control as appropriate.

Open Commission this controller safely on the controller card. Inject a load and stale feedback, change one reviewed value at a time, and explain the saturation, error, tolerance, and neutral-output evidence before applying anything to the draft.
Add kS/kV/kA and gravity feedforward only with documented units; compare the contextual commissioning result with the separate Academy control and homing teaching labs.
Define freshness, homing evidence, current monitoring, fault latching, neutral recovery, and cross-mechanism interlocks.
In Simulation & testing, inject stale feedback and a failed output write. Explain why the preview requires neutral and why simulation is not hardware approval.
Review the eight conceptual artifacts and their ownership labels before saving; generated plumbing is separate from files students may customize.
lessons.successLooksLike: The descriptor validates, the generated mock/contract tests are enabled, and you can trace input → Redux → immutable state → controller → IO without placing hardware calls in reducers.
lessons.safetyNote: Simulation and generated tests do not approve a mechanism for physical use. Verify units, limits, homing thresholds, and neutral behavior on restrained hardware later.

checkpoints.title: Draft subsystem states
checkpoints.instruction: Define named target setpoints and mechanism states in the builder.
checkpoints.successText: Subsystem states are defined.

checkpoints.title: Connect natural hardware state
checkpoints.instruction: Use the state created with each physical device and identify target versus measured values.
checkpoints.successText: The mechanism has explicit target, position, velocity, and current state.

checkpoints.title: Define safety constraints
checkpoints.instruction: Configure current limits, physical soft limits, and fail-safe neutral behaviors.
checkpoints.successText: Safety limits and neutral defaults are specified.

checkpoints.title: Preview fail-safe behavior
checkpoints.instruction: Enable generated mock/test support and use the interactive safety preview for at least one unhealthy condition.
checkpoints.successText: Mock support and generated contract verification are selected.

checkpoints.title: Review generated ownership
checkpoints.instruction: Open Review and inspect which files are starters, generated plumbing, and verification.
checkpoints.successText: The artifact ownership plan has been reviewed.

checkpoints.title: Save subsystem descriptor
checkpoints.instruction: Save the canonical subsystem specification to the workspace.
checkpoints.successText: Subsystem descriptor is saved and ready for code generation.

checkpoints.title: Trace Redux state flow
checkpoints.instruction: Explain how driver input flows through pure actions and reducers to immutable state.
checkpoints.successText: You recorded the engineering explanation in your own words and verified the supporting tool evidence.

lessons.title: Redux Unidirectional State Flow Lab
lessons.outcome: Trace a driver input signal through Redux action dispatch -> pure reducer -> immutable state -> IO write -> unit-tagged telemetry.
beforeYouStart: ARES uses unidirectional dataflow: Driver Input -> Action -> Reducer -> Immutable State -> Subsystem IO -> Telemetry.
steps: Open the State Flow interactive lab.
Dispatch a motor velocity action and inspect how the pure reducer computes the next immutable state snapshot.
Verify that previous state snapshots remain completely unchanged (immutability guarantee).
Observe the Subsystem Controller read the new state and write output voltages to the IO layer.
Inspect unit-tagged telemetry published to NetworkTables 4.
lessons.successLooksLike: You can trace any user input or autonomous command step-by-step through the entire Redux architecture.
lessons.safetyNote: Never mutate state in-place. In-place mutations corrupt multi-threaded telemetry and replay logging.

checkpoints.title: Explain state immutability
checkpoints.instruction: Why must Redux reducers return a fresh immutable state instance rather than modifying the existing object?
checkpoints.successText: You recorded the engineering explanation in your own words and verified the supporting tool evidence.

lessons.title: Homing Dwell & Latched Fault Recovery Lab
lessons.outcome: Validate sensor freshness, stall current dwell timing, latching faults, and confirmed neutral write recovery.
beforeYouStart: Mechanical hardstops can be detected via current spikes or limit switches.
A single noisy current sample must never trigger homing without sustained dwell evidence.
steps: Open the Homing & Safe Recovery interactive lab.
Configure digital limit switch homing with required debounce dwell time.
Simulate current stall homing and observe how transient current spikes are filtered.
Inject a motor output fault and observe the subsystem controller latch into a safe neutral state.
Perform a confirmed neutral write recovery sequence to clear the fault safely.
lessons.successLooksLike: You can design robust homing sequences and fault recovery routines that protect gearboxes and motors.
lessons.safetyNote: Always verify current limit thresholds in software before attempting mechanical hardstop stall homing.

checkpoints.title: Explain dwell timing
checkpoints.instruction: Why is sustained dwell time required before confirming a stall or limit switch homing event?
checkpoints.successText: You recorded the engineering explanation in your own words and verified the supporting tool evidence.

lessons.title: Review Hardware Addresses & Cached Reads
lessons.outcome: Compare canonical FTC hardware-map names or FRC CAN addresses with observed topology, then explain why sensor reads are cached once per loop.
beforeYouStart: FTC uses REV Hub / Octoquad I2C and bulk read caching.
FRC uses CAN bus (CANivore / RIO) device IDs for TalonFX and CANcoders.
steps: Open Hardware Setup and compare every canonical declaration with the observed robot or simulator topology.
For FTC, copy the exact case-sensitive configuration names into the Robot Controller configuration; drivetrain names are fl, fr, rl, and rr.
For FRC, verify every CAN ID and bus name in the vendor tools and canonical document.
Confirm the generated IO reads each device once per loop into cached values instead of reading hardware from getters.
Review the zero-allocation contract and resolve duplicate or missing addresses before build/deploy.
lessons.successLooksLike: Every required declaration has one unambiguous address and you can distinguish a reviewed configuration from a physical hardware test.
lessons.safetyNote: ARES does not pulse physical motors from this review screen. Direction testing needs a mode-gated, time-bounded robot acknowledgement and a restrained mechanism.

checkpoints.title: Explain zero-GC loop rules
checkpoints.instruction: Why must 50-100Hz control loops avoid object instantiations and iterator allocations in robotics code?
checkpoints.successText: You recorded the engineering explanation in your own words and verified the supporting tool evidence.

lessons.title: Coordinate Multi-Subsystem Robot Postures
lessons.outcome: Define named robot postures (Intake, Rest, Score, Climb) across multiple subsystem targets in Superstructure Studio.
beforeYouStart: A robot posture represents a synchronized multi-subsystem target state (e.g. Elevator high + Arm extended + Wrist tilted).
steps: Open Superstructure Studio from the navigation sidebar.
Define named postures for each game phase: Rest, IntakeGround, IntakeSubmersible, ScoreHigh, ClimbDeploy.
Assign explicit setpoints (positions, angles, velocities) for every subsystem in each posture.
Set interlock constraints to prevent arm extension while elevator is below safety thresholds.
Save the superstructure specification and preview posture setpoints.
lessons.successLooksLike: Multi-subsystem postures are defined with explicit setpoint bounds and interlock constraints.
lessons.safetyNote: Never allow simultaneous multi-mechanism motion without verifying that intermediate clearance envelopes do not self-collide.

checkpoints.title: Confirm subsystems ready
checkpoints.instruction: Verify that all required mechanism subsystems are configured in the project.
checkpoints.successText: Subsystem descriptors are loaded.

checkpoints.title: Define named postures
checkpoints.instruction: Create at least two distinct multi-subsystem postures (e.g. Rest and Score).
checkpoints.successText: Postures are defined with target setpoints.

checkpoints.title: Preview deterministic motion
checkpoints.instruction: Run the transition simulation preview across declared posture waypoints.
checkpoints.successText: Deterministic preview verified.

checkpoints.title: Verify fault injection
checkpoints.instruction: Simulate a subsystem obstruction and observe coordinated neutral latching.
checkpoints.successText: Fault injection safety confirmed.

checkpoints.title: Save superstructure specification
checkpoints.instruction: Save the completed superstructure posture configuration to the workspace.
checkpoints.successText: Superstructure specification document is saved.

checkpoints.title: Explain posture conflict resolution
checkpoints.instruction: How does the superstructure coordinator ensure conflicting mechanism states cannot execute concurrently?
checkpoints.successText: You recorded the engineering explanation in your own words and verified the supporting tool evidence.

lessons.title: 2D Stateflow Canvas & Directed Bezier Transitions
lessons.outcome: Position state nodes on the 2D canvas, configure directed cubic Bezier transitions, and verify collision-free mechanism choreography.
beforeYouStart: Open Superstructure Studio with configured subsystems.
Ensure at least two robot postures (e.g. Rest and Score) are defined.
steps: Open Superstructure Studio and toggle the top-right view to Stateflow Canvas.
Drag the posture node cards (e.g. Intake, Travel, Score) to represent your robot's physical movement hierarchy.
Inspect the directed cubic Bezier transition arrows between linked states, noting bidirectional curvature offsets.
Configure intermediate travel waypoints to prevent arm/elevator collisions during posture transitions.
Run the transition preview to verify smooth, monotonic movement without kinematic deadlocks.
lessons.successLooksLike: All robot state nodes are positioned cleanly on the 2D canvas with valid directed Bezier transitions and zero mechanical collision conflicts.
lessons.safetyNote: Never deploy a superstructure stateflow to physical hardware without verifying transition clearances in simulation first.

checkpoints.title: Position state nodes on 2D Canvas
checkpoints.instruction: Switch to Stateflow Canvas view and drag state cards into an intuitive mechanical layout.
checkpoints.successText: State nodes have explicit 2D canvas coordinates assigned.

checkpoints.title: Configure directed Bezier transitions
checkpoints.instruction: Verify that all valid state transitions have directed Bezier arrows with explicit curvature.
checkpoints.successText: Transitions are mapped between active robot postures.

checkpoints.title: Verify collision prevention locks
checkpoints.instruction: Confirm that opposing mechanism actions (e.g. wrist rotation during elevator extension) declare proper interlocks.
checkpoints.successText: Stateflow transition paths are collision-free and validated.

lessons.title: Mechanism Sizing & Current Budgeting Lab
lessons.outcome: Calculate gear reductions, stall torque margins, mechanism inertia, and total current draw against brownout limits.
beforeYouStart: A robot with four drive motors and four mechanism motors can exceed 12V battery current capacities without software budgeting.
steps: Open the Mechanism Sizing interactive lab.
Select a mechanism type (Arm, Elevator, Flywheel) and enter payload mass and arm length.
Calculate required gear reduction to operate at 40-60% of motor peak power.
Check loaded travel time and steady-state holding current under gravity.
Evaluate total robot current draw across multiple simultaneous mechanisms to verify brownout headroom.
lessons.successLooksLike: You can size motor gear reductions and current limits to prevent thermal shutdown and battery voltage brownouts.
lessons.safetyNote: Operating motors near stall torque causes rapid thermal buildup and trips circuit breakers within seconds.

checkpoints.title: Explain motor power band
checkpoints.instruction: Why should high-load mechanisms be geared to operate near 50% of free speed rather than near stall torque?
checkpoints.successText: You recorded the engineering explanation in your own words and verified the supporting tool evidence.

lessons.title: PID Feedback Response Lab
lessons.outcome: Tune Proportional rise time, Derivative damping, and Integral anti-windup to eliminate steady-state error on dynamic plants.
beforeYouStart: Proportional (kP): reduces rise time by applying force proportional to error.
Derivative (kD): dampens oscillations by resisting error rate of change.
Integral (kI): eliminates steady-state bias by accumulating error over time.
steps: Open the Control Response interactive lab.
Increase kP until the mechanism rises quickly toward the setpoint.
Observe overshoot oscillations and increase kD to introduce critical damping.
Apply an external load disturbance and observe steady-state error.
Add small kI with anti-windup clamping to eliminate steady-state offset without causing instability.
lessons.successLooksLike: You can systematically tune a PID controller to achieve fast rise time with minimal overshoot and zero steady-state error.
lessons.safetyNote: Excessive kI without anti-windup causes massive integral windup spikes when a mechanism is temporarily obstructed.

checkpoints.title: Explain derivative damping
checkpoints.instruction: How does derivative gain kD resist rapid velocity changes to prevent overshoot without adding steady-state drag?
checkpoints.successText: You recorded the engineering explanation in your own words and verified the supporting tool evidence.

lessons.title: Trapezoidal & S-Curve Motion Profiling Lab
lessons.outcome: Constrain maximum velocity, acceleration, and jerk limits for smooth, repeatable mechanism trajectories.
beforeYouStart: Step inputs demand infinite acceleration and cause wheel slip or mechanical shock.
Trapezoidal profiles bound velocity and acceleration; S-curve profiles bound jerk.
steps: Open the Motion Profile interactive lab.
Configure a Trapezoidal profile with max velocity (vMax) and max acceleration (aMax).
Observe the position, velocity, and acceleration curves over time.
Switch to S-Curve parameterization and inspect how bounded jerk smooths acceleration transitions.
Compare tracking error when feedback controllers follow a dynamic profile versus a raw step setpoint.
lessons.successLooksLike: You can generate bounded motion profile setpoints that prevent wheel slip and mechanical drive train backlash.
lessons.safetyNote: High jerk transitions damage 3D-printed gears and introduce structural resonance into gyro heading sensors.

checkpoints.title: Explain jerk limiting
checkpoints.instruction: Why does bounding the rate of acceleration change (jerk) improve mechanism repeatability and reduce mechanical stress?
checkpoints.successText: You recorded the engineering explanation in your own words and verified the supporting tool evidence.

lessons.title: Gravity & Velocity Feedforward Lab
lessons.outcome: Apply gravity compensation (kg * cos(theta)) for pivoting arms and velocity feedforward (kv) for high-inertia flywheels.
beforeYouStart: Feedforward models the physics (voltage required to hold gravity or overcome friction) before error occurs.
Feedback only acts after an error has already been detected.
steps: Open the Control Challenges interactive lab.
Select the Pivoting Arm challenge and observe the arm sag under gravity with pure PID.
Add gravity feedforward (kG * cos(theta)) to balance the arm weight across all angles.
Select the Shooter Flywheel challenge and tune velocity feedforward (kV * targetRPM).
Compare how feedforward supplies predictable model-based effort while feedback corrects remaining model and disturbance error.
lessons.successLooksLike: You can explain kS, kV, kA, and kG with units and choose an appropriate subsystem feedforward model without treating teaching-model gains as robot-ready.
lessons.safetyNote: Feedforward values must always match physical motor units (Volts per rad/s or Volts per unit load).

checkpoints.title: Explain feedforward vs feedback
checkpoints.instruction: Why does feedforward drastically improve trajectory tracking compared to relying solely on feedback error?
checkpoints.successText: You recorded the engineering explanation in your own words and verified the supporting tool evidence.

lessons.title: Run One Safe, Evidence-Guided Tuning Experiment
lessons.outcome: Turn a paired-run finding into one bounded typed change, test it in Local Sim, compare a new run, and record an accept, revise, or rollback decision.
beforeYouStart: Import the two Academy practice runs and compare them in Guided Run Review first.
A comparison can show a difference or correlation; it cannot prove that a tuning value caused it.
Guided experiments are local records. They do not change canonical profiles, generated source, or physical hardware.
steps: In Guided Run Review, choose one finding and select Create one-change experiment.
Read the original evidence timestamp, topics, explanation, and uncertainty before choosing a parameter.
Write one question and prediction, list the conditions you will hold constant, choose a success threshold before the run, and record the Local Sim safety boundary.
Choose one declared numeric PID, feedforward, motion-profile, or drive-response value and one recorded metric. ARES proposes one conservative change inside the declared bounds.
Snapshot the typed profile and canonical robot configuration. Confirm the proposed step is inside the declared bounds.
Launch verified Local Sim. For LIVE_SAFE values, apply the candidate only to the loopback simulator and wait for its explicit acknowledgement.
Open the simulator Dashboard, start the same routine, select Record run, repeat the maneuver, then select Stop & save. Only this explicit Local Sim recording is eligible as candidate evidence.
Let ARES compare the same metric without mixing timestamps or units. Read Improved, Regressed, or Inconclusive against the threshold you declared before testing.

Record Accept, Revise, Reject candidate, or Roll back, the reason, and the next safe test. Accept is available only when the recorded improvement meets the threshold and still requires a separate reviewed canonical-profile promotion.
Export the mentor/student engineering report and explain what the simulation did—and did not—prove.
lessons.successLooksLike: One saved experiment links its baseline finding, immutable configuration snapshot, bounded change, candidate run, comparison result, decision, limitations, and exported report.
lessons.safetyNote: Use Local Sim first. Guided apply is fail-closed to the loopback simulator; physical validation needs a separate documented safety procedure.

checkpoints.title: Select typed tuning target
checkpoints.instruction: Choose a declared subsystem controller parameter from the tuning catalog.
checkpoints.successText: Tuning parameter selected.

checkpoints.title: Propose bounded parameter change
checkpoints.instruction: Enter a proposed gain value within declared safety bounds.
checkpoints.successText: Valid tuning proposal drafted.

checkpoints.title: Verify proposal provenance
checkpoints.instruction: Confirm the active session ID, author, and timestamp before applying gains.
checkpoints.successText: Proposal provenance verified.

checkpoints.title: Verify telemetry response evidence
checkpoints.instruction: Record step-response rise time and overshoot percentage from live charts.
checkpoints.successText: Structured review evidence verified.

checkpoints.title: Predict system response
checkpoints.instruction: How do feedforward and feedback gains combine to produce target response?
checkpoints.successText: You recorded the engineering explanation in your own words and verified the supporting tool evidence.

checkpoints.title: State evidence boundaries
checkpoints.instruction: What are the limitations of a 1D physics preview compared to real robot mechanism dynamics?
checkpoints.successText: You recorded the engineering explanation in your own words and verified the supporting tool evidence.

lessons.title: Commission a Simulated Robot Without Overclaiming Evidence
lessons.outcome: Move one FTC or FRC project from typed controller design through fault simulation and configuration review to a clearly labeled physical-validation handoff.
beforeYouStart: Finish the drivebase and at least one mechanism controller in Robot Studio.
Use Local Sim; a simulation pass and a configuration review are not physical tests.
Physical validation remains optional and requires a supervised team procedure and a named observer.
steps: Open the subsystem commissioning sandbox and run the normal-step teaching model for the selected controller.
Inject stale feedback, a frozen heartbeat, invalid feedback, a failed write, brownout, excessive current, unconfigured hardware, and an unhomed mechanism where applicable.
Verify every unsafe case commands neutral, latches when required, and clears only after explicit successful neutral recovery.
Open Guided Tuning → SysId and run the hardware-free mechanism lesson. Explain why its kS, kV, kA, and PID values cannot be promoted to the robot.
Connect a simulator or robot runtime and confirm Studio lists only live SysId mechanisms that runtime explicitly supports. Do not proceed if capability is unknown.
Open Hardware Setup and copy the exact FTC hardware-map names or FRC CAN/channel addresses into the controller configuration.
Review motor direction, follower transforms, encoder polarity, canonical units, coordinate signs, safe neutral, limits, current monitoring, homing, calibration, freshness, and mechanical clearance.
Record the configuration review. Confirm the evidence ladder names its exact inventory hash and never calls it physical validation.
Read the four evidence levels: Simulation verified, Configuration reviewed, Ready for physical validation, and Physically validated.
If no real robot and approved procedure are available, stop at Ready for physical validation and state what remains untested.
If your team later performs the supervised real-robot checklist, record the named observer, procedure, observed result, and limitations. Editing a descriptor must invalidate that evidence.
Export or commit the `.ares` evidence with the project so mentor and student can review the same configuration revision.
lessons.successLooksLike: The project presents hash-bound simulation and review evidence, blocks unsupported live SysId, and makes the remaining physical-validation boundary unmistakable.
lessons.safetyNote: Never use a simulation result, telemetry connection, or checked form as proof of real hardware behavior. Physical motion requires the team's supervised safety procedure.

lessons.title: Author Autonomous Spline Trajectories
lessons.outcome: Build Bezier spline paths in Path Planner with independent heading targets, kinematic velocity limits, and named event triggers.
beforeYouStart: Autonomous routines combine holonomic motion splines with parallel mechanism commands (e.g. Intake on move).
steps: Open Path Planner from the navigation sidebar.
Set starting pose on the field matching your alliance's legal starting position.
Add waypoints and adjust tangent handles to shape smooth Bezier spline paths.
Decouple robot heading targets from translation tangents (holonomic advantage).
Add Event Markers along the trajectory to trigger intake deployment or shooter spinup.
Run the kinematic simulator preview to verify trajectory timing and velocity limits.
lessons.successLooksLike: A valid autonomous routine with smooth spline paths and coordinated event markers is generated and ready to run.
lessons.safetyNote: Always verify that spline paths keep the full robot bumper perimeter inside the legal field perimeter at all times.

lessons.title: Autonomous Safety & Resource Interlock Lab
lessons.outcome: Validate field boundary clearances, parallel subsystem resource locks, timeout watchdogs, and abort recovery policies.
beforeYouStart: Parallel routine steps must declare exclusive resource locks (e.g. two tasks cannot command the intake simultaneously).
steps: Open the Autonomous Safety interactive lab.
Adjust waypoint positions until the robot perimeter clips the field perimeter, and observe boundary validation failure.
Create a parallel task conflict (e.g. simultaneous Intake and Shoot) and observe resource lock rejection.
Configure step timeout watchdogs to prevent an uncompleted sensor trigger from stalling the entire 30-second autonomous period.
Select Stop-and-Report vs Continue-on-Failure policies for critical vs optional scoring steps.
lessons.successLooksLike: You can design robust autonomous routines with verified boundary clearance, exclusive resource locks, and timeout guards.
lessons.safetyNote: Every autonomous action must have a non-infinite timeout to prevent the robot from freezing indefinitely during match play.

lessons.title: Guided Run Review & Telemetry Forensics
lessons.outcome: Align two recorded runs, inspect exact timestamped evidence, and explain an observed difference without overstating its cause.
beforeYouStart: Import at least two runs from the same team, season, and robot workspace. Simulator runs are sufficient for this lesson.
steps: Open Guided Run Review from the navigation sidebar.
Select a primary run and one or more comparison runs from the same workspace.
Align the runs by recording start, autonomous start, a shared match event, or a timeline annotation.
Inspect trajectory, loop time, voltage, current, localization error, driver input, mechanism tracking, and persisted alerts where those topics exist.
Open a finding at its exact replay timestamp and verify the listed source topics.
Label your conclusion as an observation or correlation. State what additional test would be needed to establish a cause.
Export the mentor/student report without changing the original sessions.
lessons.successLooksLike: You can point to an exact timestamp and topics, describe what changed between runs, distinguish correlation from cause, and propose one safe follow-up test.
lessons.safetyNote: A historical threshold or correlation is not a diagnosis or proof that the robot is safe. Verify possible causes with approved pit procedures and independent live measurements.

lessons.title: DuckDB SQL Telemetry Forensics
lessons.outcome: Query high-speed telemetry frames using DuckDB SQL to extract peak current draws, loop overrun frequencies, and match statistics.
beforeYouStart: ARES persists all telemetry frames into local DuckDB column-store databases.
steps: Open Database Viewer from the navigation sidebar.
Inspect the `telemetry_frames` table schema: timestamp, topic, value, unit, validity.
Run a query to find peak motor currents: `SELECT topic, MAX(value) FROM telemetry_frames WHERE topic LIKE '%CurrentAmps%' GROUP BY topic`.
Query loop execution duration to identify 100Hz loop overruns.
Export query results to CSV/Parquet for post-match team review.
lessons.successLooksLike: You can write SQL queries against the local DuckDB telemetry database to extract rigorous quantitative engineering metrics.
lessons.safetyNote: Local DuckDB queries run completely offline on your laptop with zero internet required.

checkpoints.title: Explain telemetry querying
checkpoints.instruction: How does querying raw telemetry frames with SQL allow teams to find transient electrical spikes that summary graphs miss?
checkpoints.successText: You recorded the engineering explanation in your own words and verified the supporting tool evidence.

lessons.title: Graduate GUI Specs into Production Kotlin
lessons.outcome: Compile, assemble, and verify production Kotlin code for FTC Android / FRC RoboRIO with zero-GC regression tests.
beforeYouStart: All GUI-authored blueprints (Drivebase, Subsystems, Stateflow, Routines) compile into pure Kotlin season code.
steps: Open Robot Studio from the navigation sidebar.
Review the project identity, target league (FTC / FRC), and authoring stages.
Trigger the automated code generation pipeline to graduate GUI specifications into Kotlin source files.
Execute the build task (`:TeamCode:assembleDebug` for FTC or `simulateJava` for FRC).
Verify that zero-GC regression tests and unit test suites pass 100% cleanly.
lessons.successLooksLike: Production Kotlin robot code is compiled, tested, and ready for deployment to the physical robot controller.
lessons.safetyNote: Always perform a bench test with wheels raised before enabling newly generated code on a physical robot.

lessons.title: Map a Safe Driver Control
lessons.outcome: Connect a named robot capability to an explicitly mapped gamepad control, review its safety behavior, save it, and prove the generated runtime contains it.
beforeYouStart: Open a project with at least one generated subsystem capability. A physical gamepad and robot are not required.
steps: Open Driver & operator controls in Robot Studio and inspect the typed action catalog before choosing an input.
Select one visual button with a valid FTC/FRC mapping, then bind a generated subsystem action through the normal review form.
For drive axes, review deadband, sign, and response curve. For actions, review debounce, cooldown, and maximum-active policies rather than accepting them blindly.
Check capability coverage. Every required neutral-recovery or calibration action needs a direct, enabled binding; a routine reference does not count as emergency reachability.
Save the canonical control scheme, run Verify & build, and inspect the generated binding before claiming the mapping exists at runtime.
lessons.successLooksLike: A mapped platform control reaches a saved action binding, required safety actions are directly reachable, and deterministic generation succeeds.
lessons.safetyNote: A generated binding proves software wiring only. Keep the robot disabled and restrained when the physical control is first tested.

lessons.title: Read Live Pit Signals Without Overclaiming
lessons.outcome: Use a live telemetry heartbeat and named signals to find missing or suspicious evidence, then keep physical inspection and restrained testing as separate human steps.
beforeYouStart: Connect to a simulator for practice or to the disabled robot in the pit. Never enable motion from this screen.
steps: Open Pit Diagnostics from the navigation sidebar.
Confirm STREAM LIVE before trusting displayed values. A connected socket without a fresh robot-loop heartbeat is stale.
Review battery voltage and the presence of all four drive signals. Presence proves transport, not direction or safe motion.
Review odometry and vision health separately. A healthy camera with no target is different from a disconnected camera.
Open Hardware Setup to compare exact FTC hardware-map names or FRC CAN addresses with the canonical project.
Record physical checks and restrained direction tests separately; do not turn this read-only page into a match-readiness certificate.
lessons.successLooksLike: You can identify the data source, distinguish live from stale evidence, name any missing signal, and explain what still requires a person and restrained hardware.
lessons.safetyNote: This screen never commands motors and cannot certify wiring, direction, homing, CAN integrity, or match readiness.

checkpoints.successText: You recorded the engineering explanation in your own words and verified the supporting tool evidence.

lessons.title: Save and back up a robot project
lessons.outcome: Create a reviewed local version and explain why online backup is a separate optional step.
beforeYouStart: Choose a canonical ARES robot workspace and make one small reviewed change.
steps: Open Project Backup and identify the active project path before changing history.
Start local history. Explain why this does not upload the project.
Review the exact changed-file list and verify that no credentials, keystores, or local machine settings are included.
Describe the change in plain language and save the content-bound version.
If your team uses GitHub, sign in with the short device code and choose a private personal or team repository that an owner approved for ARES. Connect it only after the local project is clean.
lessons.successLooksLike: The project has a named local version, the pending change list is empty, and you can distinguish local history from optional GitHub backup.
lessons.safetyNote: Never commit passwords, OAuth tokens, signing keys, service-account files, or a robot project's local machine settings.

checkpoints.title: Explain the two backup boundaries
checkpoints.instruction: What remains only on this computer after Save this version, and what changes only after a successful GitHub sync?
checkpoints.successText: You recorded the engineering explanation in your own words and verified the supporting tool evidence.
